newsitem.title: Nigeria: Nigeria frees three as it meets Commonwealth.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria frees three as it meets Commonwealth.

text.p: Nigeria's military government on Tuesday freed three political activists held since the beginning of the year as it met a Commonwealth group charged with nudging it towards democracy and a greater respect for human rights.
The state news agency reported that lawyers Gani Fawehinmi and Femi Falana, vehement critics of the military government, were freed from jails in the north where they were being held.
Government officials said lawyer Femi Aborishade, chief strategist of Fawehinmi's unregistered National Conscience Party, had also been freed from a jail in the north.

Despite the release of the three men, many others remain in detention including Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of a 1993 presidential election whose annulment plunged Nigeria into political turmoil.

Africa's most populous nation is treated as a pariah for alleged human rights abuses and last year's hanging of nine minority rights activists including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa, which caused its suspension from the Commonwealth.

The meeting in Abuja is due to last two days and Nigeria says it is a continuation of contacts with the Commonwealth which Nigeria hopes will lead to its readmission to the club of Britain and its former colonies.

Nigerian officials said the seven ministers of the Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) would meet a broad section of Nigerian society, including traditional rulers and civil rights activists.

CMAG ministers, led by their chairman Zimbabwean Foreign Minister Stan Mudenge met behind closed doors with a 20-member Nigerian delegation led by Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi, who was hard-hitting in his opening remarks.
"Nigeria considers the immediate lifting of her suspension from the Commonwealth as the only means for restoring confidence and mutual understanding between us and the Commonwealth," he said.
"This meeting is being used to restate our position and the delegates should emphasise to the governments of the Commonwealth the need to rescind the decision of last November."
Ikimi also attacked Britain, saying remarks by British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind in a London television programme that Nigeria could be expelled from the Commonwealth, were provocative.
On the eve of the talks, the United Nations detailed serious human rights abuses in Nigeria.
The U.N. human rights report released in New York said Nigeria's military government has done little to stop summary executions, arbitrary arrests and systematic torture of political prisoners.
It gave a long list of lawyers, journalists, human rights advocates and politicians it said were killed, arrested without trial, tortured in prison or shot while demonstrating peacefully.

"Between our suspension and now many detainees have been freed and it is crystal clear that the transition is on course," said Alex Akinyele, chairman of a government commission charged with reconciling Nigeria's aggrieved groups and a member of the official delegation to the meeting with CMAG.
CMAG is made up of foreign ministers of Britain, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Ghana, Jamaica and Malaysia and its report will be submitted to the Commonwealth secretariat in London.
